subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2! In this unit you will become an explorer of shapes. Shapes are everywhere around you, and once you start to notice them you will never stop. The round moon that tells us when Ramadan begins, the square tiles on the masjid floor, the tall cylinder of a water tank in Hargeisa, the flat triangle of a folded shawl – all of these are shapes with special names and special properties. In this unit you will learn to name them, describe them, and understand how they fit together.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 2 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Identify and name common 3D shapes: sphere, cube, cuboid, cylinder and square-based pyramid.
Describe 3D shapes using the words faces, edges and vertices, and recognise curved surfaces.
Spot 3D shapes in everyday objects around your home and neighbourhood.
Identify and name 2D shapes, including the new polygons pentagon, hexagon and octagon.
Find and draw lines of symmetry (vertical and horizontal) on 2D shapes.
Create your own symmetrical patterns and designs.
Divide shapes into equal parts and name halves, quarters and three-quarters.
Tell the difference between equal and unequal parts of a whole.
Use 3D shape knowledge to work out what a shape looks like from above (its footprint).

concepts.title: What Are 3D Shapes?
concepts.explanation:
A 3D shape is a solid shape. The letters '3D' stand for three dimensions: length, width and height. A 3D shape takes up space and you can hold it in your hand. Think of a football, a sugar cube, or a tin of camel milk – each of these is solid and takes up room on the shelf.

In this unit you will meet five important 3D shapes: the sphere, the cube, the cuboid, the cylinder, and the square-based pyramid. Let us look at each one carefully and learn what makes it special.

A sphere is perfectly round, like a ball. It has no flat faces, no edges and no vertices. Instead it has just one curved surface that goes all the way around. If you roll a sphere it moves smoothly in any direction, because there are no corners to stop it. Examples you know: a football, a marble, an orange, and the globe that shows the map of the world.

A cube has 6 faces, and every single face is a square of exactly the same size. It has 12 edges and 8 vertices (corners). Because all its faces are equal squares, a cube looks the same whichever way you turn it. Examples: a dice, a sugar cube, and a child's building block. When Yusuf stacks his building blocks, he is stacking little cubes.

A cuboid also has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, just like a cube. But there is one important difference: the faces of a cuboid are rectangles, and they are not all the same size. Opposite faces match each other, but the box is longer in some directions than others. Examples: a cereal box, a book, a brick, and the box a new pair of shoes comes in. A cube is really just a special cuboid where every face happens to be a square.
concepts.example: A square-based pyramid has 5 faces: 1 square at the bottom (the base) and 4 triangles for the sides. The four triangular faces lean inwards and meet at a single point at the top called the apex. A square-based pyramid has 8 edges and 5 vertices – four corners around the square base and one more at the pointed apex. Examples: the shape of some tents, the roof of some buildings, and certain wrapped chocolates.

concepts.title: Faces, Edges and Vertices
concepts.explanation:
To describe a 3D shape well, we use three special words: faces, edges and vertices. Learning these three words carefully is the key to the whole of 3D geometry, so let us take them one at a time.

A face is a flat surface of a 3D shape. If you place a cube on the table, the part touching the table is one face, the part on top is another, and there are four faces around the sides – 6 faces in all. A face is always flat; a rounded surface does not count as a face.

An edge is the straight line where two faces meet. Run your finger along the top of a box; that sharp line is an edge. A cube has 12 edges – four around the top, four around the bottom, and four standing up the sides. Edges are the 'joins' of a shape.

A vertex is a corner, the point where edges meet. The word for one corner is vertex, and the word for more than one is vertices. A cube has 8 vertices, one at each corner. Where three edges come together, you find a vertex.

Here is the full table of properties for the five shapes in this unit. Learn it well, because you will use it again and again:

Look carefully at the last two rows. The cylinder has 2 flat circular faces plus 1 curved surface (which we do not count as a face), 2 edges where the circles meet the curved surface, and no corners at all. The sphere is the simplest of all to describe and the hardest to picture: it has no faces, no edges and no vertices – just one smooth curved surface.
concepts.example: A powerful way to understand faces is to imagine dipping one face of a shape in paint and pressing it onto paper, like a stamp. When Halima presses the face of a cube onto paper, it prints a square. When she presses the end of a cylinder, it prints a circle. When she presses a triangular side of a pyramid, it prints a triangle. Every flat 2D shape you print is one face of the solid – this is how 2D and 3D shapes are joined together.

concepts.title: 3D Shapes in Our World
concepts.explanation:
The best way to learn 3D shapes is to hunt for them in real life. Once you know the five shapes, you will see them everywhere – in the kitchen, at the market, in the masjid, and out in the fields. Let us go looking together.

Spheres: a football in the yard, an orange or a ripe mango, a marble, the round beads on a tasbih.

Cubes: a dice, a sugar cube, a child's wooden block, a small gift box that is equal on every side.

Cuboids: a cereal box, a Qur'an on the shelf, a brick in a wall, a matchbox, a refrigerator.

Cylinders: a tin of tomatoes, a drinking glass, a candle, a water tank, the tube inside a roll of paper.

Square-based pyramids: the pointed roof of some buildings, a tent, and certain wrapped sweets.

When Amina helps unpack the shopping from the Hargeisa market, she can sort it by shape: the tins are cylinders, the rice box is a cuboid, and the oranges are spheres. Sorting real things this way makes the shape names stick in your memory much better than reading alone. Try it at home tonight with whatever is on the shelf.
concepts.example: You can also build 3D shapes. You can stack small cubes to make towers and steps. You can roll and shape clay or playdough into spheres and cylinders. And you can use a net – a flat pattern of joined 2D shapes – that folds up to make a 3D shape. A net for a cube, for example, is made of six squares joined together; fold along the edges and it becomes a box. Building shapes with your hands helps you understand where the faces, edges and vertices come from.

concepts.title: 2D Shapes and Polygons
concepts.explanation:
Now we move from solid shapes to flat shapes. A 2D shape is flat and has only length and width. You already know some 2D shapes very well, and in this unit you will meet three brand-new ones. Let us begin with the shapes you know:

Circle: a perfectly round flat shape. Every point on its edge is the same distance from the centre.

Triangle: a shape with 3 straight sides and 3 vertices (corners).

Rectangle: a shape with 4 straight sides and 4 square corners; opposite sides are equal.

Square: a special rectangle where all 4 sides are the same length.

And here are the three new shapes you will learn in this unit. Notice how their names tell you the number of sides:

Pentagon: a shape with 5 straight sides and 5 vertices.

Hexagon: a shape with 6 straight sides and 6 vertices.

Octagon: a shape with 8 straight sides and 8 vertices.

All of these shapes – triangle, rectangle, square, pentagon, hexagon and octagon – share something in common: they are all polygons. A polygon is any closed 2D shape made only of straight sides. The circle is the odd one out: because its edge is curved and has no straight sides, a circle is not a polygon. A quick way to check whether a shape is a polygon is to run your finger around it. If you feel only straight lines and sharp corners, and you end up back where you started, it is a polygon. If your finger travels along a smooth curve, it is not.
concepts.example: You can also count sides to name a polygon. If Farah draws a shape and counts 6 straight sides, she knows at once it is a hexagon, even before she looks at it closely. The bees that make honey build their honeycomb out of hexagons, because hexagons fit together neatly with no gaps – a lovely example of geometry in nature.

concepts.title: Symmetry and Lines of Symmetry
concepts.explanation:
Symmetry is one of the most beautiful ideas in all of mathematics. A shape has symmetry when it can be divided into two parts that are exact mirror images of each other. The line that divides the shape into two matching halves is called a line of symmetry.

Imagine folding a shape in half along a line. If the two halves land exactly on top of each other, with no part sticking out, then that fold line is a line of symmetry. This is why folding paper is the simplest way to test for symmetry. Khadija folds a paper heart down the middle; the two halves match perfectly, so the heart is symmetrical.

There are two lines of symmetry we name by their direction:

A vertical line of symmetry goes straight up and down, like a person standing tall.

A horizontal line of symmetry goes straight across, from side to side, like a person lying down.

You can test any shape for symmetry in three ways: fold it along a line and see if the halves match; place a mirror on the line and see if the reflection completes the shape; or draw a line and check that each side is the mirror of the other. All three tests give the same answer.

Different shapes have different numbers of lines of symmetry. This is a wonderful thing to explore, because the more regular a shape is, the more lines of symmetry it has:

Infinite (any line through the centre)

4 (vertical, horizontal, and two diagonal)

Do you notice a pattern? A regular polygon – one where all the sides and corners are the same – has exactly as many lines of symmetry as it has sides. A regular pentagon has 5 sides and 5 lines of symmetry; a regular hexagon has 6 of each; a regular octagon has 8 of each. The circle, which is perfectly round, has infinite lines of symmetry, because any straight line through its centre divides it into matching halves.
concepts.example: You can also create your own symmetrical patterns, which is great fun. Draw a line of symmetry, make a design on one side, then copy that design as an exact mirror image on the other side. This is just like folding a piece of paper, cutting a shape, and unfolding it to reveal a design that matches on both sides. Many traditional patterns and decorations use symmetry to look balanced and pleasing to the eye.

concepts.title: Turning and Flipping Shapes
concepts.explanation:
The same shape can look different depending on how it is turned or flipped. This is an important idea, because a triangle standing on its point looks different from one sitting on its base – yet it is still the same triangle.

When we turn a shape around, we call it a rotation. When we flip a shape over, like turning a page, we call it a reflection. Some shapes look exactly the same no matter how you turn them: a circle always looks like a circle, however you spin it. Other shapes look different when turned: a triangle pointing up is easy to tell apart from a triangle pointing down.
concepts.example: Here is something worth thinking about carefully. If Omar turns a square a little, it may look like a diamond, but it is still a square – the sides and corners have not changed, only the direction it faces. Learning to recognise a shape even when it is turned or flipped is a real mathematical skill, and it stops you from being tricked. A shape keeps its name no matter which way it points.

methods.title: How to describe a 3D shape
methods.example: A tin of tomatoes has two circular flat ends and one curved surface around the middle. What 3D shape is it?
steps: Count the flat faces (do not count curved surfaces).
Count the edges — the lines where faces meet.
Count the vertices — the corner points.
Say the shape's name and its three numbers.

methods.title: How to find a line of symmetry
methods.example: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have?
steps: Imagine folding the shape in half along a line.
Check whether the two halves match exactly.
If they match, that line is a line of symmetry.
Try vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines to find them all.

methods.title: How to divide a shape into equal parts
methods.example: A cube is sitting on a table. One face is flat on the table and hidden. How many faces can you see?
steps: Decide how many equal parts you need (2 for halves, 4 for quarters).
Draw lines so that every part is the same size.
Check the parts are equal by comparing them.
Name each part: one-half, one-quarter, or three-quarters.

methods.title: Name the polygon
methods.example: Sagal draws a closed shape with 6 straight sides. What is it called?
steps: A closed shape with 6 straight sides is a hexagon.
(Remember: 5 sides is a pentagon, 6 is a hexagon, 8 is an octagon.)
Check by counting the sides again — a hexagon always has exactly 6.

methods.title: Count lines of symmetry
methods.example: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
steps: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: one vertical, one horizontal, and two diagonal.
You can fold it along any of these four lines and the halves will match exactly.

Noor cuts a rectangle into two pieces.

workedExamples.title: Name the 3D shape
workedExamples.prompt: A tin of tomatoes has two circular flat ends and one curved surface around the middle. What 3D shape is it?
workedExamples.solution: Two flat circular faces joined by a curved surface, with no corners, describes a cylinder. So the tin is a cylinder.

workedExamples.title: Count faces, edges and vertices
workedExamples.prompt: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have?
workedExamples.solution: Count slowly. A cube has 6 faces (top, bottom, and four sides), 12 edges (four around the top, four around the bottom, four standing up), and 8 vertices (one at each corner). So the answer is 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.

workedExamples.title: Hidden faces
workedExamples.prompt: A cube is sitting on a table. One face is flat on the table and hidden. How many faces can you see?
workedExamples.solution: A cube has 6 faces in total. One face is hidden against the table. So you can see 6 − 1 = 5 faces.

workedExamples.title: Name the polygon
workedExamples.prompt: Sagal draws a closed shape with 6 straight sides. What is it called?
workedExamples.solution: A closed shape with 6 straight sides is a hexagon. (Remember: 5 sides is a pentagon, 6 is a hexagon, 8 is an octagon.)

workedExamples.title: Count lines of symmetry
workedExamples.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
workedExamples.solution: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: one vertical, one horizontal, and two diagonal. You can fold it along any of these four lines and the halves will match exactly. Worked Example 6: Halves or not? Noor cuts a rectangle into two pieces. One piece is large and one is small. Has she made halves? Solution: No. To make halves, the two parts must be exactly equal in size. Because one piece is large and one is small, they are unequal parts, not halves.

workedExamples.title: Halves or not?
workedExamples.prompt: Noor cuts a rectangle into two pieces: one large and one small. Has she made halves? Explain.
workedExamples.solution: No. To make halves, the two parts must be exactly equal in size. Because one piece is large and one is small, they are unequal parts, not halves. Noor would need to cut the rectangle so both pieces are exactly the same size for them to be true halves.

workedExamples.title: Sharing into quarters
workedExamples.prompt: Four children share a square pizza equally. What fraction does each child get, and how should the pizza be cut?
workedExamples.solution: Four equal shares means quarters. Cut the pizza with one line down and one line across to make 4 equal parts. Each child gets one-quarter (¼) of the pizza.

workedExamples.title: Shape from above
workedExamples.prompt: Liban looks straight down on a cylinder standing on its end. What 2D shape does he see?
workedExamples.solution: Looking down on a cylinder, he sees its circular top face, so the footprint is a circle.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: A shape is cut into 2 equal parts. What is each part called? What about 4 equal parts?
workedExamples.solution: 2 equal parts = halves; 4 equal parts = quarters.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Name the curved-surface shapes among: cube, sphere, cylinder, cuboid.
workedExamples.solution: Sphere and cylinder have curved surfaces.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: How many faces are hidden when a cuboid sits on its largest face?
workedExamples.solution: 5 faces hidden? No — 1 face is hidden (the one on the table); 5 are visible.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: A regular hexagon has how many lines of symmetry? What about a regular octagon?
workedExamples.solution: 1) Regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry; regular octagon has 8.

activities.title: 3D Shape Hunt
activities.materials: your home, and a pencil and paper to record what you find.
steps: Walk through the kitchen and living room looking for 3D shapes.
Find at least one sphere, one cube, one cuboid and one cylinder.
Write the name of each object next to its shape name.
Ask a family member to add one more object to each shape group.
Keep your list. You will be surprised how many shapes hide in an ordinary room!

activities.title: Face Printing
activities.materials: a few solid objects (a tin, a box, a block), some paint or a stamp pad, and paper.
steps: Choose one object and press one flat face onto paper to print its shape.
Name the 2D shape you printed (a square, a rectangle, a circle, a triangle).
Try every different face of the object and print each one.
Say which 3D shape each print came from.
This shows you how the flat faces of 3D shapes are really 2D shapes.

activities.title: The Symmetry Mirror Game
activities.materials: a small mirror (or shiny spoon), paper, and a pencil.
steps: Draw a shape such as a square, a heart, or a butterfly.
Stand the mirror upright on a line through the middle of the shape.
If it matches, you have found a line of symmetry. Try other lines too.
This game trains your eye to spot symmetry quickly – a skill artists and tailors use every day.

activities.title: Fair Sharing Investigation
activities.materials: a round anjero or a square piece of bread, and a knife (ask an adult to help).
steps: Start with one whole piece of food and estimate how to cut it fairly for two people.
Cut it into 2 equal parts. Check that the parts are the same size – these are halves.
Now cut each half again to make 4 equal parts – these are quarters.
Talk about what happens to the size of each part as you cut more pieces.
You have just turned sharing food into a lesson about fractions and equal parts.

activities.title: Shape Guessing Game (Family Game)
steps: One player secretly chooses a 3D or 2D shape.
That player describes it without saying its name: ‘I have 6 square faces and 8 corners.’
Everyone else guesses the shape from the clues.
Take turns so everyone has a chance to describe and to guess.
Describing shapes with the right words – faces, edges, vertices, sides – makes the game fair and helps everyone learn.

activities.title: Build a Shape With Cubes
activities.materials: four small cubes (sugar cubes, blocks, or clay cubes you make yourself).
steps: Use all four cubes to build a shape – a tower, an L-shape, or a square.
Write down how you made it, using words like 'on top of' and 'next to'.
Read your instructions to a partner and see if they can build the same shape.
Did your partner use the correct words? How could the description be clearer?

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand shapes best? What was the trickiest part – counting edges, finding symmetry, or making equal parts? What would you like more practice with? Share your answer with your teacher at your next session, or with your AI tutor right away if your teacher is not available.

rules.title: Faces, Edges and Vertices Rule
rules.text: A face is a FLAT surface. A curved surface is not a face. An edge is a line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner point where edges meet.

rules.title: Polygon Rule
rules.text: A polygon is a closed 2D shape with only straight sides. Count the sides to name it: 5 = pentagon, 6 = hexagon, 8 = octagon. A circle is not a polygon because its edge is curved.

rules.title: Fraction Rule
rules.text: The parts must be EQUAL in size. Two equal parts = halves. Four equal parts = quarters. Four quarters make one whole; three-quarters means 3 of 4 parts.

terms: A solid shape you can hold
Flat surface / line join / corner point
A rounded surface that is not flat
A closed 2D shape with straight sides
The fold line making two matching halves
One of 2 / one of 4 equal parts
commonMistakes: Counting a curved surface as a face

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Symmetry and Lines of Symmetry.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Symmetry is one of the most beautiful ideas in all of mathematics. A shape has symmetry when it can be divided into two parts that are exact mirror images of each other. The line that divides the shape into two matching halves is called a line of symmetry.

Imagine folding a shape in half along a line. If the two halves land exactly on top of each other, with no part sticking out, then that fold line is a line of symmetry. This is why folding paper is the simplest way to test for symmetry. Khadija folds a paper heart down the middle; the two halves match perfectly, so the heart is symmetrical.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Turning and Flipping Shapes.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
The same shape can look different depending on how it is turned or flipped. This is an important idea, because a triangle standing on its point looks different from one sitting on its base – yet it is still the same triangle.

When we turn a shape around, we call it a rotation. When we flip a shape over, like turning a page, we call it a reflection. Some shapes look exactly the same no matter how you turn them: a circle always looks like a circle, however you spin it. Other shapes look different when turned: a triangle pointing up is easy to tell apart from a triangle pointing down.
